title: Taking the light
hookLine: Krishna eats Sudama's handful of rice; why the arti flame comes back to everyone
carry: what you offer comes back as grace
last: HARI — THE ONE WHO TAKES THE TROUBLE AWAY.

lines: A POOR MAN AT A PALACE GATE.
A HANDFUL OF RICE IN A RAG.
cards: A poor man stands outside a palace gate in Dvaraka, holding a small bundle of flattened rice tied in a rag. His wife begged it from the neighbors. Inside lives Krishna, his old friend from school, now a king.
Who brings a handful of rice to a king? But the gates open, and Krishna runs out, hugs him, washes his feet, and sits him on his own bed. Then he smiles and asks: so, what did you bring me?

teach.h: KRISHNA EATS THE RICE WITH DELIGHT.
teach.b: The friend is usually called Sudama, and the story is in the Bhagavata Purana. Sudama hides the bundle. He's ashamed.
Krishna takes it from him anyway, opens it, and eats a handful with delight, as if it were the best food in the palace.
In the telling, he says he gladly accepts even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, when it's offered with love. Sudama walks home without asking for a thing.
When he gets there, his hut has become a house full of plenty. He gave a handful. It came back as grace.

teach.h: PRASAD: WHAT COMES BACK IS GRACE.
teach.b: Hindus have a word for what comes back: prasad, grace. You met it with the laddus: food is offered at the shrine, then shared out as a blessing. Arti works the same way, with light.
When the song ends, the lamp that was just circled before the divine is carried out to everyone.

teach.h: HANDS OVER THE FLAME, THEN TO THE EYES.
teach.b: You cup your hands over the flame, close enough for warmth, never touching, then bring your hands to your eyes, your face, sometimes over your head.
That's taking the light: receiving the blessing back. A few customs travel with it. An arti flame usually isn't blown out; blowing on a sacred flame is often seen as disrespectful.
And if you're a guest and unsure, watch first, then copy the person beside you. The light is offered to everyone in the room, the way Krishna treated a poor friend's handful as a king's gift.

how: At the end of arti, the lamp is brought to each person, who passes cupped hands over the flame without touching it and then touches the hands to the eyes, face or head; in temples, people often place a small offering on the plate as it passes.

o: light, the flame taken from the arti plate
a blessing whispered over a newborn
the ash a flame leaves behind on the plate

games.q: the rice and the flame — tap the pairs.
p: brings a handful of flattened rice
eats it as if it were a feast
what comes back to you as grace
then to the eyes and head

s: Krishna was embarrassed by Sudama's small gift
he ate it with delight. what mattered was the love it was offered with.
after arti, the flame is carried out to the people
the light offered before the divine comes back to everyone, like prasad.
you're meant to touch the arti flame
hands pass over it, close enough for warmth, never touching.

games.q: you're Sudama at the palace with a rag of flattened rice. Krishna asks what you brought. what does the story say to do?
o: hide it. a king won't want it.
hand it over. offered with love, it's accepted.
go home and come back with something better.
games.why: Krishna ate the rice with joy, and Sudama came home to plenty. that's prasad: what's offered comes back as grace, the way the arti flame comes back to every hand.

practice: If it's safe, light a candle or lamp; if not, picture the arti plate coming toward you.
Cup your hands and pass them slowly over the warmth, a few inches above, never touching, then draw them back and rest your palms softly over your closed eyes, feeling the warmth there.
Once more, and this time let your hands pass over the top of your head, then rest them in your lap and stay with the flame.

wordCard.voice: Jyoti, the flame: after arti it comes back out to the people, and hands pass over it to the eyes and the head, taking the light as grace. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit jyoti: light, flame. The light people take from the arti plate.

carryVoice: Your line: what you offer comes back as grace. Sudama gave a handful; the light comes back to your hands. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.80–10.81 (Krishna and his poor brahmin friend, known as Sudama)
Receiving the arti flame, as practiced in home and temple worship
